question_text: If a ray makes angles α, β, γ, δ with the four diagonals of a cube then show that cos²α+cos²β+cos²γ+cos²δ = 4/3.

recall_prompt: Say how you would prove this — say how many diagonals a cube has, and what identity collapses the sum.

steps.label: Set the cube on the axes
steps.margin_note: First mark. Nothing in the question fixes a cube, so one is CHOSEN: put a vertex at the origin and three edges along the axes. Angles do not change when the cube is moved, so this placement is allowed; every coordinate is then 0 or a, and the side a cancels at the end.
steps.memory_tip: Choose the cube: vertex at the origin, edges along the axes. The side a cancels at the end.

and edges coincide with the coordinate axes.
Let A, B, C be the vertices of the cube on the x-axis,
y-axis, z-axis so that OA = OB = OC = a

recall.must_convey: That the cube is placed with a vertex at the origin and edges along the axes.
accept: put one vertex at the origin and the edges along the axes

steps.why: Placing the cube on the axes is allowed, since the angles do not depend on where the cube is placed, and makes every vertex a triple of 0's and a's. The answer is a pure number, so a must cancel — and it does.
common_mistakes: Using different edge lengths, which is not a cube.

steps.label: Write all four diagonals
steps.margin_note: Two marks. A cube has FOUR body diagonals, and the question needs all of them. Each joins a vertex to the one diagonally opposite through the body.
steps.memory_tip: A cube has FOUR body diagonals and the question needs all of them.

steps.why: A cube has exactly four body diagonals, one for each of the four pairs of opposite corners. Drawing them helps you see all four.
common_mistakes: Drawing only two diagonals; this question needs all four.
Counting face diagonals among the four.

steps.label: Find cosα for the first diagonal
steps.margin_note: Two marks. Let the ray have direction cosines (l, m, n), so l² + m² + n² = 1 — that identity is what makes the denominator √3·a.
steps.memory_tip: The ray's own l² + m² + n² = 1 is what makes the denominator √3·a.
lines: Let (l, m, n) be the d.c's of the given ray,
then we have l² + m² + n² = 1
The ray makes angles α, β, γ, δ with OP, CL, NB, AM

lines.text: (the angle between the ray (l, m, n) and OP (a, a, a);
the modulus is left out, since cos²α is

lines: ∴ cosα = (al + am + an) / √((a²+a²+a²)(l²+m²+n²))

lines.text: (a² + a² + a² = 3a² and l² + m² + n² = 1)

recall.must_convey: That with l² + m² + n² = 1 the first cosine is (l + m + n)/√3.
accept: let the ray have direction cosines l m n so their squares add to one
cos alpha is l plus m plus n over root three
the a cancels and the root of the sum of squares is one

steps.why: l² + m² + n² = 1 is the defining property of direction cosines, and using it here is what removes the second factor from the denominator entirely.
common_mistakes: Treating (l, m, n) as direction RATIOS, whose squares need not add to 1.

steps.label: Write the other three by symmetry
steps.margin_note: One mark. The other three diagonals differ only in signs, so their cosines are the same expression with signs changed — no new working is needed.
steps.memory_tip: The other three differ only in SIGNS, so no new working is needed.

lines.text: NB (−a, a, −a) and AM (−a, a, a))
\cos \gamma \ = \ \dfrac{ - l\ + \ m\ - \ n}{\sqrt{3}},\ \cos \delta \ = \ \dfrac{ - l\ + \ m\ + \ n}{\sqrt{3}}

recall.must_convey: That the other three cosines are (l+m−n)/√3, (−l+m−n)/√3 and (−l+m+n)/√3.

steps.why: Each diagonal's sign pattern carries straight into its cosine, which is why one calculation serves for all four.
common_mistakes: Recomputing each from scratch and slipping a sign.
Giving all four the same expression.

lines_compact.text: \cos \gamma \ = \ \dfrac{ - l\ + \ m\ - \ n}{\sqrt{3}},\ \cos \delta \ = \ \dfrac{ - l\ + \ m\ + \ n}{\sqrt{3}}

steps.label: Add the four squares
steps.margin_note: Two marks (the last two). Pair the four terms and use (a+b)² + (a−b)² = 2(a² + b²) on each pair, then once more on (l+m)² + (l−m)² — the cross terms cancel and (4/3)(l² + m² + n²) is left, with l² + m² + n² = 1.
steps.memory_tip: Pair the terms and use (a+b)² + (a−b)² = 2(a² + b²) on each pair, then on (l+m)² + (l−m)² — the cross terms cancel.
lines: ∴ cos²α + cos²β + cos²γ + cos²δ
= ⅓[(l+m+n)² + (l+m−n)² + (−l+m−n)² + (−l+m+n)²]

lines.text: ((−p)² = p², so (−l + m − n)² = (l − m + n)²

lines: = ⅓[(l+m+n)² + (l+m−n)² + (l−m+n)² + (l−m−n)²]

lines.text: (pair the first two and the last two)

lines: = ⅔[(l+m)² + (l−m)² + 2n²] = ⅔[2(l² + m²) + 2n²]

recall.must_convey: That pairing the squares gives (4/3)(l² + m² + n²) = 4/3.
accept: add the four squares and use a plus b squared plus a minus b squared is twice the sum of squares
everything collapses to four thirds times l squared plus m squared plus n squared
since that is one the answer is four thirds
naalugu squares add chesthe four by three vasthundi

steps.why: The identity is applied to the pair carrying (l+m), to the pair carrying (l−m), and then to (l+m)² + (l−m)² — every cross term cancels, leaving a result that does not depend on the ray at all.
common_mistakes: Expanding one of the four squares with a sign slip, so the cross terms do not cancel.
Forgetting that l² + m² + n² = 1 at the last step.

insider_note: All four body diagonals are needed here, not one pair. Pair (l + m + n)² with (l + m − n)² and (l − m + n)² with (l − m − n)², use (a + b)² + (a − b)² = 2(a² + b²) on each pair and then on (l + m)² + (l − m)², and l² + m² + n² = 1 gives the answer.
